activity: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
knowledge_domain: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
fact: Bones show up white on an X-ray because the calcium in them absorbs more X-rays than the softer tissue around them.
story:
Isla sat on the bench at the edge of the soccer field with her X-ray printout balanced on her good knee. Her left arm, wrapped in a bright green cast, rested in her lap, and every few minutes the coach blew the whistle and she had to remind herself she wasn't supposed to run out there. Evelyne plopped down beside her, dusty from drills, and leaned over the film.

"Why do your bones look like glowing white sticks?" Evelyne asked. "Your arm and everything else is just a gray smudge."

Isla held the film up against the sky. The two bones of her forearm stood out sharp and pale, and the break near her wrist made a crooked line she couldn't stop staring at. "The doctor said something about it," she said slowly. "Something in the bones. I think it's the calcium. The calcium absorbs more of the X-rays than the softer stuff around it, so the bones show up white and everything else barely shows at all." She turned the film over, as if the answer might be printed on the back.

"Calcium, like in milk," Evelyne said.

"Like in milk." Isla looked down at her cast, and an idea clicked into place. When they'd taken the X-ray, the thick part of the cast had shown up faintly on the image too, a hazy white shadow behind the bone. Old plaster casts had calcium in them. That was why the technician had angled the machine around it. Her idea wasn't just a guess; the same stuff, the same white glow. "I'm going to ask Martha," she said. "She broke her wrist last year. If her old X-ray shows the cast shadow too, then I'm right."

They found Martha by the goal net, breathing hard while Ms. Sato called out instructions to regulate the pace of the scrimmage. Ms. Sato saw Isla's awkward one-armed attempt to carry her water bottle and jogged over to open it for her, then stayed to fan Martha with a clipboard until she caught her breath. Martha dug out her phone, scrolled through photos, and held up her own X-ray. There it was: the bone, brilliant white, and behind it the ghostly outline of her old cast.

"So the calcium drinks up the X-rays," Martha said, "and whatever drinks up the most shows up brightest."

"The tendon doesn't, though," Isla said, pointing at the thin gray thread of tissue near Martha's wrist. "That's why you can barely see it." She flexed the fingers of her casted hand, the last voluntary movement the doctor had allowed her, and grinned. "Three more weeks, and I'm back on that field."

Ms. Sato handed her the whistle. "You can officiate until then," she said. "First call of the scrimmage, right there."

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: Muscles grow stronger during recovery after training, not during the workout itself, so rest days are part of getting better.
story:
Jonathan had one goal for the season: beat Connor at everything. Connor was the fastest kid on the team, and he knew it, which made beating him even more satisfying in theory. In practice, Jonathan kept coming in second, which was getting old.

Then something strange happened at Tuesday practice. Mr. Sow set up sprint drills, and Jonathan beat Connor. Twice. Connor bent over, hands on his knees, and stared at the grass like it had insulted him. "I've been training every single day since March," he said. "Morning jog, afternoon sprints, evening juggling. I'm the most diligent soccer player in this county." He said it like a badge, but he looked like a melted snowman.

On Thursday, Jonathan beat him again, and this time Atlas noticed too. "You're getting slower," Atlas told Connor, with the kindness of a friend and the delivery of a game show host. "Like, measurably." After practice, Jonathan rode his bike home puzzling over it. Training every day should make you faster, shouldn't it? Unless the getting stronger part happened somewhere he couldn't see, some hidden step between the workout and the speed. His own week suddenly looked interesting: Monday sprints, Wednesday practice, and in between, honestly, a lot of video games and a heroic amount of cheese crackers. He had been resting. A lot. And he had been getting faster.

Friday, he tried an actual test, in the scientific tradition of making stuff up. "Connor," he said, dropping a soccer ball on the bleachers next to him, "take two days off. No jogging, no sprints. Total sloth mode." Connor looked personally wounded. "My legs will forget how to be legs." "Two days," Jonathan emphasized, holding up two fingers. "Then we race Saturday." Connor grumbled, but he agreed, mostly because losing to Jonathan had made him agree to anything.

Saturday morning, the field was still damp and the nets sagged like tired hammocks. Atlas stood at the sideline with a stopwatch he had borrowed from Mr. Sow, who watched from the parking lot with his coffee and one raised eyebrow. They raced sideline to sideline, three times. Connor won the first by a full stride. He won the second by two. On the third, he crossed the line, spun around, and pointed at Jonathan. "You knew! Rest days are part of getting better, you sneaky little scientist!" Jonathan raised both arms like he'd won the World Cup. "Race you to the water bottles," said Connor.

activity: to improvise a scene with a partner by accepting each offer with yes, and
knowledge_domain: to improvise a scene with a partner by accepting each offer with yes, and
fact: Blocking is rejecting or ignoring a partner's offer, such as saying 'we're not on a boat', and it usually stops the scene from moving forward.
story:
Chase sat on the living room rug with his notebook open, because on Monday he and Yuna had to perform a two-minute improv scene in drama class, and so far every practice had collapsed. Yuna knelt across from him, drumming her fingers on the coffee table.

"Okay," she said. "I'm the captain of a boat."

"There's no boat," Chase said. "We're in a supermarket."

Yuna slumped. "Right. Again."

Chase frowned at his notebook. He thought about Tuesday, when Brent had gone up in front of the class and pretended to toss a ball to a kid, saying, "Fetch, boy!" The kid had answered, "No, that's not my dog," and the whole room went quiet, like someone had pulled a plug. Brent had stood there holding an invisible leash until Mr. Warsame called time. At the time Chase had laughed, but now he wondered whether the same thing was happening to him and Yuna. It was like there was a hidden rule, something you couldn't see, deciding which scenes lived and which ones died. Both times, somebody had refused what the other person offered, and the scene just stopped.

"Let's simulate it," Chase said. "You say the boat thing again, and instead of fighting it, I'll say yes and add something."

Yuna straightened up. "I'm the captain of a boat."

"Yes, and the hull is porous," Chase said, patting the rug, "so we're bailing water with these buckets."

Yuna's eyes lit up. "Yes, and there's a tsunami coming, so we'd better bail faster."

"Yes, and I see an island to the north."

They went back and forth, trading offers, and the scene rolled along like a wheel downhill. A pirate appeared, then a talking seagull, then the seagull turned out to be the coast guard. Chase realized he'd been wrong earlier. He'd thought a good scene meant winning, keeping his own idea on top, but it worked the opposite way. The scene got better when he let go of his plan and built on hers.

"Wait," Yuna said, grabbing his arm. "I get it. When you said 'there's no boat,' that was blocking." She said the word carefully, the way Mr. Warsame had said it once in passing. "Blocking. That's what it's called."

"Then no more blocking," Chase said. He flipped his notebook to a fresh page and wrote the words YES, AND across the top in big letters, underlined twice, then tore it out and taped it to the coffee table where they couldn't miss it.

Yuna picked up her invisible bucket and grinned. "Bail faster, sailor. That wave's getting closer."

activity: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
knowledge_domain: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
fact: Placing onion cells in salty water draws water out of them, so the cell membrane shrinks away from the cell wall and can be seen; this is called plasmolysis.
story:
Beatrice set the microscope case on the flat rock beside the creek and knelt to open it, because Mr. Gauthier had said the seventh-grade trail lab counted the same as a classroom lab, and her grade in science needed the help. Her job was to peel a paper-thin layer from an onion, mount it on a slide, and label three parts: the cell wall, the membrane, and the nucleus. The wall she could see already, brick-shaped boxes in neat rows. The nucleus showed up as a dark dot once she added the stain. The membrane was the problem. It lay so flat against the wall that it might as well have been invisible, and her diagram, worth half the marks, had an empty arrow pointing at nothing.

Aveer crouched beside her with the field kit, holding a dropper bottle of plain creek water and, in his other hand, a second bottle he had filled from his own lunch, the salty water left over from his pretzels. "You could just evaluate what you've got," he said, squinting through the eyepiece. "Draw the wall, draw the nucleus, and take the partial marks."

"I need the whole diagram," Beatrice said. She thought about it while a jay screeched somewhere up the slope. She had a hypothetical idea, the kind Mr. Gauthier liked: if the membrane was pressed flat against the wall like a wet shirt on a window, maybe it would show if something pulled it loose. She didn't know what could pull it, but she knew she could test the idea fast. "Give me your pretzel water."

"You want my spit-water on your slide?"

"It's just salt water. Hand it over." He did, and she laid one careful drop at the edge of the coverslip and watched it seep under. For a moment nothing changed, and she held her breath, afraid she had flooded the whole slide and ruined everything. Then, slowly, row by row, each cell seemed to shrink from the inside. Something thin and clear peeled away from every brick-shaped wall and crumpled toward the center, like a balloon letting go of the inside of a box. The arrow on her diagram finally had something to point at.

Agam came over from the tree station to see why she was grinning. "What happened to them?"

"Salt water pulls the water out of the cells, so the membrane shrinks away from the wall," Beatrice said, already sketching. "Aveer says it's called plasmolysis."

"It's on the poster in the classroom," Aveer admitted. "I read it this morning."

Beatrice laughed and wrote the word across the top of her page, then bent back to the eyepiece to catch the last row before the light shifted. "Draw fast," she said, holding out a pencil to Agam.

activity: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
knowledge_domain: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
fact: Like terms can be combined before solving, so 2x + 3x becomes 5x, but 2x and 3 cannot be combined because one has a variable and one does not.
story:
Vincent stared at the whiteboard in Ms. Ito's room like it had personally insulted him. The problem was 2x + 3x = 15, and beside him Charlize was already flipping her paper over to start the next one.

"Five x equals fifteen," Vincent said. "So x is three. Done."

Amine leaned over. "Show your work, or Ms. Ito will call it reckless guessing again."

"It's not guessing, it's confidence." Vincent wrote 2x + 3x = 5x anyway, because Amine had a smug face when he was right.

Then the next problem appeared: 2x + 3 = 11. Vincent wrote 5x = 11 without slowing down, and his hand hovered there while something in the back of his brain raised a small polite objection. He frowned at his paper. In the first problem, two x's and three x's were both x's, so they went together fine. But the three in this new problem was just a three. There was no x attached to it. He tried imagining x as a box of pencils. Two boxes plus three boxes made five boxes, sure. Two boxes plus three loose pencils made two boxes and three pencils, and that was that.

"You look like you bit a lemon," Charlize said.

"I wrote something weird." He showed her the 5x = 11. "Is that legal?"

Charlize tapped the 3. "What's the x attached to there?"

"Nothing. It's just three." Vincent erased the 5x and wrote 2x + 3 = 11 again, untouched, feeling a bit foolish and a bit brilliant at the same time. So you couldn't smash them together. Two x plus three stayed two x plus three, and you had to deal with it some other way. He thought about the balance scale Ms. Ito kept on her desk, the one she'd used to argue that whatever you did to one side you owed the other side. Subtract three from both sides. That left 2x = 8, and then x = 4. He checked it: two times four plus three did make eleven. He did a tiny drumroll with his pencil, which flew out of his hand and rolled under Amine's chair.

"Nice hygiene," Amine said, picking it off the floor and wiping it on his sleeve before handing it back.

"That's not what hygiene means."

"Whose pencil landed on the floor?"

Ms. Ito walked past and glanced at Vincent's paper. "I see you and the three are no longer on speaking terms."

"We oppose each other," Vincent said. "It has no x, and I stand for x rights."

She smiled and moved on, and Vincent started the next problem, writing slowly this time, checking every term for hidden x's like a detective. "Four x plus one x plus seven," he muttered. "Five x, plus seven, and the seven just gets to sit there being seven."

activity: going away to summer camp for the first time
knowledge_domain: going away to summer camp for the first time
fact: The American Camp Association was founded in 1910, under the name Camp Directors Association of America, to set common standards for organized camps.
story:
The dining hall smelled like bacon and pine floor wax, and Charlotte held her tray at the edge of the room, unsure where to sit. It was her first day at Camp Whippoorwill, her first time away from home for more than a weekend. A girl with a sunburned nose waved her over. "You're in Cabin Four, right? I'm Emmie. Sit here."

At the gate that morning, Charlotte had noticed a wooden sign by the office: Accredited by the American Camp Association. She'd asked the counselor driving the van what it meant, and he'd answered while shifting gears. "American Camp Association. It was founded in 1910, under the name Camp Directors Association of America, to set common standards for organized camps." Charlotte had filed that away. Standards meant rules, and rules meant things got counted and checked, which struck her as useful information about any place she was going to live in for two weeks.

The problem appeared at lunch on Wednesday. Every table got chocolate chip cookies, and the counselor at the serving window called out that each table's share was proportional to its head count, two cookies per camper. Cabin Four had ten campers. They got sixteen cookies. Charlotte counted twice, sliding the plate away from the girl who was already reaching. On Thursday, the same thing: ten campers, seventeen cookies. On Friday, fifteen.

"You're going to perceive a pattern here or you're not," Emmie said, watching Charlotte line up the numbers in ketchup on her tray. Charlotte had a theory. Nobody was miscounting, because the count happened in one place, the window, and the shortage happened after, at the table. She thought it through: if cookies vanished between the window and the table, the cause had to be somewhere along that short trip. So she tested it. She volunteered to carry the plate on Saturday.

She walked slowly and watched. At the far end of the third bench, Anson from Cabin Six slid his hand out and lifted two cookies with the ease of a small-time entrepreneur who had been running this scheme all week. He'd figured out that new campers were too busy being nervous to count anything, and that everyone blamed the kitchen.

Charlotte set the plate down, leaned over, and said, "You owe Cabin Four eleven cookies."

Anson turned pink. The camp director, Ms. Patel, was wiping down the next table, and she looked up at the word "owe." When Charlotte explained, counting on her fingers, Ms. Patel nodded toward the window. "The kitchen counts every batch," she said. "Ask them. It'll match." It did: twenty cookies baked for that table, fifteen on the plate.

At dinner, a plate of eleven cookies arrived at Cabin Four's table, carried by Anson himself, handed over without a word. Emmie took the first one and broke it in half.

activity: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
knowledge_domain: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
fact: The bandwagon technique urges people to do or buy something because "everyone else is," appealing to the wish to belong rather than giving a reason.
story:
Joseph flopped onto the couch in the living room and adjusted the pillow behind his back just as the commercial started. A famous streamer he recognized, DexRaven, held up a glowing headset and said, "I never game without ThunderPulse. It's legendary." Then the screen filled with a huge crowd of people, all wearing the same headset, while a voice boomed, "Join the millions who already switched to ThunderPulse. Don't get left behind with extinct, outdated gear."

"That's the one," Maxim said from the armchair, leaning forward. "Everybody at school is getting them before the tournament. If we don't switch too, we're basically playing in the Stone Age." Joseph looked at the price in the corner of the screen and felt his stomach drop. It cost more than he had saved in four months of mowing lawns.

He muted the TV and stared at it, chewing his thumbnail. "Wait. What does it actually do better?" Maxim shrugged. "It's just... better. DexRaven uses it." Joseph grabbed the remote and rewound the ad, watching it again with the sound low. "Notice how it never says one thing the headset does? It says millions switched, and it calls our old stuff extinct and outdated, and it shows famous people. Those are all about making us feel like losers if we don't buy it. None of it is a reason."

Ms. Hoang, their neighbour, had let herself in through the back door to return a casserole dish, and she paused in the doorway, listening. "Sounds like the bandwagon technique," she said mildly, setting the dish on the coffee table. "Urging you to do something because everyone else supposedly is, so you'll want to belong." She waved and headed back out before Joseph could ask her anything else.

"That," Joseph said, pointing at the door. "That's the name for it. Bandwagon." He pulled out his phone and looked up the headset's actual specs, then looked up his own. Same driver size. Same frequency response. Almost the same weight. The only real difference was the coloured lights on the earcups. "So my inference is the ad costs more than the extra tech does," he said slowly. "They spent all that money on a streamer and a crowd shot instead of making it better."

Maxim slumped back, disappointed. "So everybody's buying lights." Joseph unmuted the TV, where a new ad was already promising that everyone was switching to a different brand of energy drink. He tilted the remote toward it. "Look at this one and tell me what it says the drink actually does." Maxim leaned in and squinted at the screen.

activity: to build a web page with HTML and style it with CSS so the heading is centred
knowledge_domain: to build a web page with HTML and style it with CSS so the heading is centred
fact: When two CSS rules of equal specificity set the same property, the one written later wins; this ordering is part of the cascade in Cascading Style Sheets.
story:
Zoe typed `h1 { text-align: center; }` at the top of her style sheet, saved the file, and hit refresh. The big blue heading that said ZOE'S GUIDE TO ORCA WHALES stayed stuck against the left edge of the page like it hadn't heard her at all.

"That's the third time," Barrett said from the next laptop. "Maybe center just doesn't work on headings."

"It works on yours." Zoe pointed at his screen, where GLIDERS OF WORLD WAR II floated neatly in the middle of his page. Hers was the only one clinging to the margin, and she felt a flicker of resentment toward the whole language of CSS. She hadn't even wanted the fancy gradient background that Cedrick kept bragging about; she only wanted one heading, centred, like everybody else's.

Cedrick leaned over, chewing his pencil. "Maybe it's haunted."

"Maybe you're haunted." Zoe scrolled through her file anyway. The heading rule was at the top, plain as anything. Below it were rules for the background, the paragraphs, the images, and at the very bottom, way down where she'd been experimenting an hour ago, sat a line she'd forgotten: `h1 { text-align: left; }`. She stared at it. Both rules said something about the same heading, and hers was first, which should mean it counted first, shouldn't it?

She decided to hypothesize, out loud, because that was what Ms. Dlamini kept telling them to do. "What if the last one wins? What if CSS reads top to bottom and whatever comes later is what sticks?" It sounded backwards, like the last person in line getting the prize, but it was easy to test. She deleted the bottom line, saved, and refreshed. The heading slid to the center of the page so smoothly it was almost smug.

"Whoa," Cedrick said. "It was hiding down there the whole time."

"I read about that somewhere," Barrett said. "It's called the cascade. Later rules beat earlier ones."

Ms. Dlamini wandered past their row and glanced at Zoe's screen, at the blue heading sitting dead center. "Nice work. What did you change?"

"Order," Zoe said. "The last rule was winning the whole time." She put the deleted line back on purpose, refreshed, and watched the heading jump left again. Then she deleted it once more and it hopped back to center. Proof, twice.

By the end of club, she had added a centered subtitle, a centered caption under her orca photo, and, at the very bottom of her style sheet, in a comment she wrote for her future self: nothing about text-align after this line, Zoe, nothing.

activity: to improvise a blues solo over a twelve-bar chord progression
knowledge_domain: to improvise a blues solo over a twelve-bar chord progression
fact: A blues in the key of A is usually played with the chords A7, D7 and E7, which are dominant seventh chords.
story:
Maya's grandfather kept his old guitar in the hallway closet, and by Sunday afternoon she had claimed it. The recital at the community hall started at seven, which gave her three hours to learn something she had promised the music teacher she could do: improvise a blues solo. Her friend Ross was already set up at the upright piano in the living room, where the afternoon light made everything look tranquil except the two of them.

"Key of A," Ross said, playing a low A to lock it in. "So what are the chords?"

Maya stared at the frets. At home she had practiced with a backing track, and it always worked, but the track had chosen the chords for her. She plucked an A and it sounded right, deep and satisfied, but when Ross tried a minor chord under it, the whole room soured. "No," she said. "Try that one but with the seventh on top." She hummed the note she meant, and Ross found it. The chord suddenly slouched, like it had somewhere better to be.

"That's it," Maya said. "A7. Blues chords want that sound." They hunted for the other two the same way, Ross sliding his hands around the keyboard while she tested notes on the guitar. D7 came next, then E7, and when Ross played all three in a loop, twelve bars at a time, it sounded like actual blues, the kind her grandfather put on the record player while he cooked.

The problem was the solo itself. Every time the E7 came around, Maya froze and played nothing, because at home the track had hidden which chord was which. Here she could see Ross's hands, so she made a deal with herself: watch the hands, and when they jumped to the chord built on E, play fewer notes, save the big bend for right there. She tested it once through and missed, tested again and landed it, and the miss itself told her something. The chords weren't decoration under the melody. They were the ground the melody walked on, invisible unless you looked sideways.

Ross's little brother wandered in, turned the thermostat down to sixty, and wandered out, which meant the piano room would soon be freezing, since Grandpa's furnace took its time. "Fifteen minutes, then we pack up," Ross said, shaking feeling back into his fingers.

On the last run-through, Maya closed her eyes over the E7 and the bend came out clean, hanging in the cold air like it might never evaporate. At the hall that evening, her grandfather sat in the front row. Afterward he said only, "A7, D7, and E7. You found them yourself?"

"With some help," Maya said, and Ross bowed from the piano bench.

activity: getting through an evening power cut at home
knowledge_domain: getting through an evening power cut at home
fact: A full freezer holds a safe temperature for about 48 hours without power, and a half-full one for about 24 hours, if the door stays closed.
story:
The lights went out just as Michael was reaching for the freezer door, and his hand froze in the dark. "Mom, the power's out," he called. She came down the hall with her phone flashlight, and they stood together in the kitchen, listening to the fridge's hum die away into silence.

"The food," his mom said. "That freezer is full of everything for the week." Michael closed the door without opening it, then stopped himself. He had opened it, just once, just a crack, to peek. He told himself a crack didn't count, but the thought kept nagging him.

He went to the window. Across the courtyard, the whole apartment building across the street was dark too, and the streetlights were off, so it wasn't just their building. He knocked on the wall the usual way, and a minute later Daisy knocked back from next door. On the third floor he could see a candle in Nour's window, wobbling.

"Half an hour before you opened that door," his mom said, sitting on the couch with a blanket. "You have to stop opening it." Michael got his notebook and, by phone light, wrote down what he knew: a full freezer holds a safe temperature for about 48 hours without power, but a half-full one only lasts about 24 hours, if the door stays closed. He'd read that in the booklet that came with the freezer, back when it was delivered, and had thought it was boring then. Now it mattered. The problem was, their freezer was half full at best. His mom had been planning a big grocery run for Saturday, and today was only Thursday. Twenty-four hours, then, if nobody opened the door again.

He thought about that crack he'd made. It was too late to undo, but he could make the rest of the time count. "Daisy," he said through the wall, "do you have ice?" She laughed. "Our freezer's dead too, genius." But then she said she'd ask her mother about the ice trays, and Nour shouted down the stairwell that her family had two bags of ice from a party. Michael counted on his fingers. If they packed the empty top half of the freezer with Nour's ice, the space wouldn't be half empty anymore. It wasn't quite full, but it was closer.

The stairwell was pitch black. He climbed by feel, one hand on the cold railing, keeping his spine straight against the wall so he wouldn't miss a step. Nour met him at her door with both bags, and Daisy came up behind him carrying her ice trays wrapped in a dish towel. Back in his kitchen, they compressed the ice into every gap around the frozen peas and the bread and the endangered chicken that was supposed to be Sunday dinner. Michael shut the door firmly and taped a note on it: DO NOT OPEN UNTIL POWER IS BACK.

Saturday morning the lights came on with a click, and the fridge started humming again. Michael peeled off the note, opened the freezer, and the cold air rolled out over his face. "Still frozen," he reported. "Every bit of it." Daisy leaned in and poked a bag of peas. "Okay," she said, "I take back what I said about your boring freezer booklet."

activity: to explain how the Treaty of Versailles helped lead to the Second World War
knowledge_domain: to explain how the Treaty of Versailles helped lead to the Second World War
fact: In March 1936, Hitler sent German troops into the Rhineland, breaking the Treaty of Versailles, and Britain and France did not use force to stop him.
story:
Cooper had four index cards, one encyclopedia open to the letter V, and no idea how to start his presentation. The assignment was on the screen of the library computer in green letters: explain how the Treaty of Versailles helped lead to the Second World War. He knew the treaty had punished Germany after the First World War, but "helped lead to" was the part Mr. Fortin would actually grade.

Sarah-Maude slid into the chair across from him with her own stack of books. "I'm doing the same topic," she said. "Jeanne found a whole chapter in this one. Want to split it?"

"Only if you explain the middle part," Cooper said. "I can get from the treaty to Germany being angry. I can't get from angry to war."

Jeanne arrived carrying a photocopy. "Listen to this," she said, and read aloud in a low voice because they were in the library. "In March 1936, Hitler sent German troops into the Rhineland, breaking the Treaty of Versailles, and Britain and France did not use force to stop him."

"That's it?" Cooper said. "That's the middle?"

"That's a piece of it," Jeanne said. "I don't know what it means either."

While they argued, a boy from their class, the one who always sat near the window, opened a bag of chips behind the reference shelf. Food in the library was against the rules. Mr. Fortin was checking books at the desk ten feet away, and he looked up, and he looked back down at his scanner. Nothing happened.

Cooper watched the boy eat the whole bag without hiding it. Then the boy got up, wandered to the display of new paperbacks marked DO NOT REMOVE UNTIL FRIDAY, and put three of them in his backpack.

"Mr. Fortin," Cooper said, before he decided to say it. "He's taking the new books."

Mr. Fortin went over, had a quiet conversation, and got the paperbacks back. The boy got a warning and a call home. Cooper sat down again, and something clicked into place. "That's the Rhineland," he said.

Sarah-Maude frowned. "The what?"

"The chips," Cooper said. "The rule got broken once and nothing happened. So he tried a bigger one. Britain and France let the first break go in 1936, when it was just troops going into the Rhineland. After that, why would he stop?" He pulled a blank card toward him and wrote rapidly. "It's not that the treaty made the war happen by itself. It's that every time somebody broke it and nobody stopped them, the rules kind of eroded. Wore down. Like a path."

Jeanne turned the photocopy around. "It says here the treaty also made German civilians pay reparations, money taken from ordinary people, not just the government. So they were angry and humiliated."

"So you get anger, then a test, then no pushback," Cooper said, arranging his cards in a line across the table. "Anger, test, nothing. Then more."

Sarah-Maude laughed. "It's ironic. The treaty was supposed to prevent another war by keeping Germany weak, and it basically handed Hitler his script."

Cooper stood and asked Mr. Fortin if he could sign out the projector cart for fifth period on Thursday. Mr. Fortin wrote his name on the clipboard. "What's your topic?" he asked.

"How the Treaty of Versailles helped cause the Second World War," Cooper said. "And how you have to stop the first broken rule, or you'll be stopping the second one a lot harder."

On his way back to the table, he passed the window seats. The boy from class was there, and he looked at Cooper for a long second, then zipped his backpack shut and left it on the floor, empty, next to his chair.

activity: babysitting a neighbor's child for the first time
knowledge_domain: babysitting a neighbor's child for the first time
fact: Shaking a baby can cause serious brain injury, because an infant's neck muscles are too weak to support its heavy head.
story:
Luke had agreed to watch the neighbor's baby for one hour, and for the first forty minutes it had gone fine, mostly because the baby slept in the stroller while Luke sat on a bench near the duck pond. Then the baby woke up and started to cry, and kept crying, and Luke's careful bouncing and patting did nothing at all.

Josie and Channing showed up right about then, which was lucky and unlucky at the same time. Channing had his tablet out because he was filming a video of the ducks for the park's summer contest, and he wanted to win more than anything. "Only one entry gets shown at the nature center," he said, crouching in the invasive vines by the fence to get a low angle. "Mine has to be the one." Josie, who had three younger cousins, took one look at the baby and said, "Have you tried the soother?" Luke found it in the stroller pocket, but it had rolled under the wheel, right through a patch of goose droppings, and there was no way he was putting something like that in the baby's mouth. Every microbe in that park was probably on it now. He envied Josie for how calm she looked, like crying babies were just weather to her.

The crying got louder. Luke's arms ached, and a hot, frustrated feeling rose up in him, and he caught himself jiggling the baby harder than he meant to, a sharp frustrated shake. Right then a Canada goose stalked over and snatched Channing's sandwich out of his open backpack, and in the chaos of Channing yelling "Not the cheddar!" Luke noticed the flyer taped to the bench arm. It was about crying infants. He read it while the baby howled: never shake a baby, because an infant's neck muscles are too weak to support its heavy head, and shaking can cause serious brain injury.

His stomach went cold. He stopped the jiggling instantly, laid the baby flat and buckled safely into the stroller, and stepped three paces away to breathe, exactly like the flyer said to do if you felt overwhelmed. Josie stood beside him. "You okay?" "Yeah," Luke said. "Just need a second." Behind them, Channing was still chasing the goose, which was not going to give back the sandwich.

And then, in the sudden quiet, the baby stopped crying. Not because of anything Luke did. The goose had come back to strut past the stroller, and the baby stared at it, fascinated, and made a small huffing sound like a laugh. Channing froze, tablet still running, and the contest footage caught the whole thing: his goose, mid-heist, and a laughing baby. "That's the shot," Channing whispered. "That is absolutely the shot."

activity: to run an eight-hundred-metre race pacing the first lap so there is energy for the second
knowledge_domain: to run an eight-hundred-metre race pacing the first lap so there is energy for the second
fact: The 800 metres draws on aerobic energy, which uses oxygen, and anaerobic energy, which works without oxygen but runs out quickly, so it feels like a sprint and a distance race at once.
story:
The wind turbine beyond the far curve of the track turned in slow, lazy circles, and Charles watched it while he waited for his heat to be called. He had signed up for the eight hundred metres because Mr. Pereira had put a blank line on the sign-up sheet and dared anyone to try something new. Nikola, the fastest sprinter in grade seven, had written his name underneath. So had Meera, who won every long-distance race the school had ever held. Charles had written his name last, mostly so the sheet would not look lonely.

In the first time trial, Nikola exploded off the line as if the gun owed him money. He led the whole first lap, arms pumping, and then, halfway down the back straight of the second lap, he simply folded. He slowed to a jog, then a walk, and finished with his hands on his knees. "It's like my legs turned to sand," he told Charles afterward. "The first lap felt easy. Easy!" Meera ran her trial the opposite way, drifting along at the back so gently that she looked bored, and when she finally kicked on the last lap she had nothing left either. She was caught at the line and finished fourth, and her look at the finish clock was nearly venomous.

Charles could not stop thinking about it on the walk home. Both of them had run one good lap and one bad one, in opposite directions. That was a pattern, and patterns had causes, even when you could not see them. He remembered a poster in the science wing about two ways the body makes energy. One kind, called aerobic, uses oxygen and lasts a long time. The other kind, called anaerobic, works without oxygen but runs out quickly. The eight hundred needed both at once, which was why Nikola had burned through his fast fuel in one lap and Meera had saved so much she never spent it.

On Saturday he tested it. He asked a parent to stand at the two-hundred mark with a watch, then ran the first lap deliberately controlled, not sprinting and not strolling, like a turbine turning at a steady speed instead of a gust. He wanted to calibrate the pace by feel, so that the first lap used the oxygen kind of energy and saved the quick kind. On the second lap his legs ached, but there was still something left in them, and he finished faster than his first trial by four seconds.

Monday at practice he found Nikola and Meera at the long-jump pit. "It's like a sprint and a distance race at once," Charles said. "You have to feed both engines. Spend the fast stuff only at the end." Meera squinted at him, then at the track, then went to find her shoes. Nikola jogged to the start line and stood there, tapping his toes against the rubber, waiting for them.

activity: to paint a portrait in watercolour by layering washes from light to dark
knowledge_domain: to paint a portrait in watercolour by layering washes from light to dark
fact: In traditional transparent watercolour, the brightest highlights, like the shine in an eye, are usually made by leaving the white paper unpainted rather than adding white paint.
story:
Evelyn had decided that the eye gleam was the soul of a portrait, the tiny white spark that made a painted face look back at you. She was seven washes into her watercolour of Kadence, who sat across the art room table posing like a very patient queen, when she noticed the disaster. Her sixth wash, a pale shadow of violet meant for the eyelid, had crept sideways and swallowed the little spot of white paper she'd been guarding for the gleam.

"That's the third time you've sighed like a dying dragon," Kadence said. "What happened?"

"I flooded the light. The eye's gone dark all the way through." Evelyn held the paper up to the window. The spot where the gleam should be was a soft grey, like a window with the curtain drawn. "I can't wash it out. Watercolour doesn't lift that clean once it's soaked in."

Brody leaned over from the next table, where he was painting what he claimed was a dragon but looked like an angry avocado. "Just put white paint on it. I have white. Take my white."

Evelyn squeezed a dab onto her palette and tried it on the corner of a scrap first, which was the kind of thing Ms. Santos-Reyes was always suggesting. She painted a shadow, dabbed white over it, and frowned. The white sat on top like chalk, dull and flat, nothing like the shining paper around it. She tried a second dab, thicker. Worse. It looked like a smudge of toothpaste. "White paint isn't the same," she said slowly. "It's cloudy. The real shine on the rest of the paper is just... paper."

She turned the scrap over and over, testing the idea from every angle like a detective. If the brightest white came from untouched paper, then she could deduce something important: highlights had to be planned before the first brushstroke, not rescued afterward. They weren't something you added. They were something you protected, right from the start. Which meant her portrait of Kadence had a villain after all, and the villain was her own impatient brush, sweeping through territories it had promised to spare. Every painting, she thought, hid its antagonist inside the painter's wrist.

"So is it fixable?" Kadence asked. "Or is my face doomed to look like a haunted doll?"

"Starting over is one option," Evelyn said. "Doing surgery with white paint is another, and we've seen how that ends." She considered whether it was feasible to carve the spot back to bare paper with a tiny bit of sandpaper, but she could already picture the scuffed fuzz it would leave, and a fuzzy eye was sadder than a dark one. She pulled a fresh sheet from the pile. "New plan. I draw your eyes first, and before any wash touches this paper, I paint a ring of masking fluid around the gleams. Like a fence. Like a fortress around the light."

Ms. Santos-Reyes drifted past and looked at the ruined portrait, then at the new sheet with its two small amber circles drying over each pupil. "Saving the paper's own shine," she said. "Smart."

The fortress held. Wash by wash, violet and rose and deep brown climbing from light to dark, the amber dots shed paint like tiny umbrellas, and when Evelyn peeled them off with her fingertip at last, two clean white sparks sat in Kadence's eyes, gleaming exactly where they had always meant to.

"It's like you're watching me," Kadence said. "It's like you're actually in there."

Evelyn propped the portrait against the paint rack and stood back, and the painted Kadence stared back at her, alive with light she'd never once had to invent. "The paper was on my side the whole time," she said. "I just had to get out of its way."

activity: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
knowledge_domain: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
fact: Historians still do not know who fired the first shot at Lexington in April 1775; British and colonial witnesses each said the other side fired first.
story:
The last slice of pecan pie vanished from the kitchen counter sometime between the touch football game and the fireworks Louis's uncle was illegally setting up in the driveway. Louis had been counting on that slice all afternoon, and he took the loss personally.

He began his investigation at the scene. The counter held a fork in the sink, a smear of filling on the edge, and a pie plate wiped cleaner than anything else in his grandmother's house, which was saying something. His cousin Meliane, who wanted to be a lawyer, insisted Kendrick had done it because Kendrick had been in the kitchen right before everyone noticed. Kendrick, who wanted to be left alone, said Meliane had gone in for ice, and that in fact she had been in there twice.

"You were in the kitchen," Meliane said.

"So were you," said Kendrick.

Louis wrote both statements in his notebook, which he had brought for a history assignment. That was the problem with the assignment, actually. Ms. Janssen had given the history club two eyewitness accounts of the morning at Lexington in April 1775, and the two accounts flatly disagreed. The British witnesses said the colonists fired first. The colonial witnesses said the British fired first. Both sides had been standing on the same green watching the same morning, and after all this time, historians still did not know who fired the first shot. Louis had stared at the papers for an hour, waiting for one of them to blink.

He tried an experiment now. He brought Meliane and Kendrick into the kitchen, both of them complaining, and reenacted the afternoon as best he could. Kendrick demonstrated where he had stood getting his soda, on the far side of the refrigerator, with his back half turned. From there the counter was blocked by the plumbing of the hanging pot rack, a thick tangle of hooks and copper bottoms. Meliane's path from the ice machine, though, had a clear view, and she had been carrying a dish towel, and there was a smudge of pecan filling on the dish towel, which was currently folded over a chair like evidence hiding in plain sight.

"Meliane," Louis said.

"I was going to bring it out for everyone," she said, which was not a denial. Her audience dwindled to zero as Kendrick drifted toward the door, uninterested in justice now that it wasn't aimed at him. Louis looked at his notebook, then at the towel, then at the empty plate, and thought about how two witnesses on one green could swear opposite things and both believe themselves completely. He underlined the towel in his notes.

"Deal," Meliane said suddenly. "Half my Easter candy for the last slice next time."

Louis shook her hand.

activity: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
knowledge_domain: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
fact: In science, a theory is not a guess; it is an explanation that has been repeatedly tested and supported, while a hypothesis is an idea still being tested.
story:
The cookies came out flat as coasters, and Abigail needed to know why. She slid the tray onto the counter and stared at the sad, crispy circles. Her little brother had made a batch yesterday from the same recipe, and his had been puffy and golden.

"Maybe the oven hates me," her brother said, grabbing a flat cookie anyway.

"The oven doesn't hate you. Something made them collapse, and I'm going to find out." Abigail flipped through her notebook until she found a blank page. "In science you start with a hypothesis. It's a testable guess. You don't just say 'cookies fail.' You say why you think they failed, then you test it."

He rolled his eyes. "Like evolution? That's just a theory, so it's just a guess."

"That's not what theory means." She tapped her pencil on the counter. "A theory is an explanation that's been tested over and over, and every test so far has backed it up. Evolution is that kind. A hypothesis is an idea still being tested, like mine about these cookies. Huge difference."

"Fine, detective. What's your hypothesis?"

Abigail looked at the two mixing bowls sitting in the sink, hers and his. Both had sticky residue, but hers had a translucent film smeared across the rim, glossy and faintly cloudy, like fogged glass. Butter. She remembered scooping hers soft and melty from a bowl that had sat near the stove while the oven preheated. Warm butter, she guessed, had wrecked the structure before the cookies even hit the pan.

"My hypothesis: if the butter is too soft, the cookies go flat. If I use cold butter, everything else the same, they should puff up." She wrote it down, underlined it twice, and texted Diego, because experiments were better with witnesses.

Diego arrived in eleven minutes flat, still holding his bike helmet. "I brought the notebook for official observations," he announced, and Abigail pointed him to a stool.

They made one small batch with butter straight from the fridge, firm enough that the spoon left clean marks in it. As the cookies baked, a thin vapor rose from the oven vent and the whole kitchen smelled like Saturday morning. Abigail crouched at the oven door, watching the dough through the glass. The edges went translucent, then golden, and the centers puffed into soft domes.

"They're rising! Diego, they're rising!" She flung the oven open at the timer's buzz and slid the tray out. Twelve rounded, puffy cookies, warm and tall.

Her brother bit into one and chewed slowly. "Okay, so cold butter. Your guess was right."

"My hypothesis was supported," Abigail corrected, grinning. She wrote the result in her notebook, then paused, pencil hovering. "But one batch isn't tested over and over. So what does that make it?"

Diego leaned over her shoulder. "Still a hypothesis?"

Abigail smiled and started measuring flour for round two. "Exactly. Science needs seconds."

activity: getting a first pair of glasses
knowledge_domain: getting a first pair of glasses
fact: The earliest eyeglasses were made in central Italy around 1290.
story:
The clock on the dashboard read 4:41, and Victoria's dad kept saying "We'll make it, we'll make it" like a chant that could change traffic. The optical shop closed at five, and if they missed tonight, her new glasses would sit in a drawer all weekend, and she would spend two more days squinting at the whiteboard while Miriam whispered what Mr. Haile had written. Victoria stared out the window, where the street signs were soft gray blobs with fuzzy edges, and tried to guess what they said anyway. The one with two round shapes was probably the school crossing. The tall skinny one might be a speed limit. It was like a puzzle where half the pieces were melted.

"I still can't believe you found out you needed glasses from a poster," Miriam said from the back seat.

Yesterday, Mr. Haile had taped a chart of letters on the classroom wall and asked everyone to read the bottom row for a health unit. Victoria had gotten stuck after the first two letters, and Mr. Haile had tilted his head and said, "Hmm." That single "Hmm" had started everything: the eye doctor, the letter E that looked like a smudge, the words nearsighted and minus two. Now the glasses were ready, waiting in a little case at the shop, and the clock said 4:47.

"I've been wondering something," Victoria said as they turned onto Main Street. "If people have always had bad eyes like me, how did anyone read before glasses were invented? Did they just... not read?" Miriam said she had no idea. Victoria had looked it up the night before, while waiting for her dad to finish filling out forms, and she wanted to test whether she remembered it right. "I think I read that the earliest eyeglasses were made in central Italy around 1290. So before that, everyone was basically me." She thought about monks copying books letter by letter with eyes like hers, holding pages at arm's length. "That's like seven hundred years of glasses. But everything before 1290, nothing."

"It's like the dinosaurs," Miriam said. "Complete extinction of tiny letters."

Victoria laughed. "Tiny tropical fish in textbooks. Extinct."

Her dad swung into the parking lot at 4:56, and Victoria was out of the car before he had fully stopped. Inside, the optician found her case, and Victoria lifted the glasses out slowly, like they might dissolve. She slid them on.

The world snapped into focus. Price tags, crisp and mean. A tropical fish poster by the register, every scale sharp. Miriam's face, with actual eyelashes.

"Okay," Victoria said, reading the smallest line on the wall chart across the room. "Now somebody delegate me a book with tiny print."

activity: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
knowledge_domain: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
fact: In Chinese culture, a clock is usually avoided as a gift, because the phrase 'giving a clock' sounds like a phrase about attending someone's death.
story:
Christopher knocked twice on Drew's front door, then remembered his own mother's rule about knocking hard, and knocked softer the second time. Drew's house always smelled like lemon polish, and today the kitchen table was covered with newspaper, a roll of wrapping paper, and a small brass wall clock in a box.

"Nice, right?" Drew said, turning the box so the clock face caught the light. "It's for the Chens. They moved in next door Friday, and Mom said we should bring a housewarming gift when we visit tomorrow. The clock was on sale." He began cutting the paper in lush green sheets with snowflakes on them, humming like a job half done.

Christopher didn't hum. He was thinking about the word the clock made in his head. Last month his cousin had married into a Chinese family, and at the wedding Christopher had watched his uncle put a clock back on the shelf at the store, fast, like it was hot. When Christopher asked why, his cousin had leaned close and said the one thing he remembered now: "In Chinese culture, a clock is usually avoided as a gift, because giving a clock sounds like a phrase about attending someone's death." Christopher had thought it was strange then. He thought it was very useful now.

"Wait," he said. "Before you wrap that. What if it's the wrong thing, like, exactly the wrong thing, for this family?" He laid out his reasoning like steps: the Chens were a Chinese family, the clock was a gift, and if the sound of "giving a clock" landed badly, then the Chens would open the box tomorrow and hear something awful inside a kind present. It was a hidden rule, the kind you couldn't see on the object itself. Drew frowned at the clock, then at the snowflake paper. "So we test it," Christopher said. "Call Ms. Malik. She grew up across the street from the Chens' cousin." He said it as a question, not a lesson, and Drew was already dialing.

Ms. Malik answered on the second ring, and Drew held the phone flat between them. "A clock?" she said. "Oh no, my mother would have fainted. Pick something else, boys." When they hung up, Drew sat still for a moment. "That would have been terrible," he said. "The irony is I picked it because it was the nicest thing I could afford." Christopher shrugged. "You picked it because you wanted their new place to feel like home. That part's still good. We just need a different homey thing."

They pooled their money, biked to the corner store, and came back with a heavy ceramic bowl painted with fish. The next evening, when Mrs. Chen opened her door, she took the bowl with both hands, the way you take something that matters, and Drew bowed a little, copying her. She laughed, called something over her shoulder, and held the door wide. "Come in, come in, we'll eat."

activity: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
knowledge_domain: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
fact: A checkable claim can be false; 'The Eiffel Tower is in Berlin' is a wrong factual claim, not an opinion.
story:
Arianna leaned over the crickets in the glass terrarium at the back of Ms. Anderson's science room and counted them twice. Fourteen yesterday, twelve today. Two crickets did not just vanish, she thought, so where did they go? Bo crouched beside her, chin on his fists.

"Maybe they escaped," Bo said. "That's my opinion, anyway."

"It can't be an opinion," Arianna said slowly. "It's a claim. We could check it. There'd be crickets on the floor or holes in the lid." She tapped the mesh. No holes. No dried little bodies behind the water dish either.

Oaklyn drifted over from the rock display, holding her notebook. "You two are weirdly excited about missing crickets." She peeked into the tank. "Oh, I bet something ate them. That's just my opinion, so you can't say I'm wrong."

Arianna remembered last month, when Oaklyn had insisted the Eiffel Tower was in Berlin and ended the argument with those same words: it's just my opinion. Ms. Anderson had overheard and frowned, and after class Arianna had looked it up on the classroom computer until the fact finally clicked in her head. The Eiffel Tower is in Berlin was a checkable claim, and it was false, plain and simple. An opinion was more like crickets are gross, which nobody could prove right or wrong. Bo hadn't been there for that, so she turned to him now. "A false claim isn't an opinion. It's just a wrong claim. The Eiffel Tower is in Berlin is a wrong factual claim, not an opinion."

"So my escape theory could be wrong," Bo admitted. He checked the lid again anyway, thorough as a detective.

Arianna prioritized the possibilities: escape, or something inside the tank eating them. She studied the terrarium. One of the "decorative" rocks she'd borrowed from the display had come from the pond behind the school, and yesterday she'd noticed a small bulge tucked in a hollow of it. Now she wondered. "Oaklyn, get the magnifier." Oaklyn flipped a rock over and the bulgle uncurled, a beetle the size of her thumbnail, jaws like tiny hooks. "Predatory," Oaklyn whispered, delighted and horrified at once. "That thing is absolutely predatory."

They reported everything to Ms. Anderson, who raised an eyebrow at the pond rock. "Well," she said, "you've turned a mystery into an experiment. What's your next step?"

"We keep the beetle in a separate container with one cricket," Arianna said, already reaching for a jar, "and watch what happens." Behind them, Oaklyn sneezed twice and wiped her eyes. "Great," she muttered. "I have an allergy to your new class pet."

activity: falling out with a best friend and making up
knowledge_domain: falling out with a best friend and making up
fact: The term 'active listening' was introduced by psychologists Carl Rogers and Richard Farson in 1957; it means trying to understand the speaker's point of view, often by repeating their meaning back in your own words.
story:
Lea sat on her bedroom floor with her phone face down beside her, like it might explode. Chiara had not answered three texts, and at school she had walked right past Lea's locker with her eyes fixed on the hallway clock, which was strange because Chiara never looked at clocks, she looked at people. Something had gone wrong, and Lea could not see what it was, which was the worst part. If she could see the crack, she thought, she could at least figure out where to press.

She replayed Thursday in her head. There had been the group project meeting in the library, where Mr. Dang had asked Lea to be the team's ambassador to the other seventh-grade class. Lea had said yes, and Chiara had gone quiet, and after that they had not really talked. But quiet was not the same as angry, and Lea kept circling the afternoon like a detective with no fingerprints. She even made a list on the back of her science notes: things I did, things I said, things I did not notice. The third column was the longest, which did not help.

On Saturday morning she wandered into the living room, where her mom had left a stack of library books on the coffee table. One was thick and pale blue, about listening, of all things. Lea flipped it open mostly out of boredom, and a line stopped her: the term "active listening" was introduced by the psychologists Carl Rogers and Richard Farson in 1957. It meant trying to understand the speaker's point of view, often by repeating their meaning back in your own words. Lea read it twice. She had been composing apologies all morning, long speeches about how sorry she was, and none of them had room in them for Chiara's side of anything.

She tested the idea out loud, alone in the living room, which felt ridiculous. "So you felt like I got picked and you got skipped," she said to the empty couch. Then she tried it another way, trying to guess what the moment must have looked like from Chiara's chair in the library: her best friend saying yes to a solo job, fast, without a glance sideways. Lea picked up her phone and typed, can you come over. Then she added, I won't do a big speech, I promise.

Chiara came at two, standing on the porch with her jacket zipped to her chin even though it was warm. They sat on the living room floor where the books still lay, and Lea's prepared apology started to rise in her throat and she pushed it down. Instead she said, "I read this thing this morning. It's called active listening. You basically say back what the other person means."

"Sounds like something a teacher would make up," Chiara said, but she unzipped her jacket.

"So," Lea said, and made herself keep going, even though her face felt hot. "When Mr. Dang picked me, you felt like I got chosen over you. Like I would rather prioritize some ambassador job than be on your team."

Chiara stared at her for a second, and then her whole posture loosened, shoulders dropping like a cut string. "That's exactly it," she said. "You didn't even look at me first."

"I didn't know," Lea said. "But I should have."

"I didn't want to be jealous about it," Chiara said. "That's why I didn't say anything. It felt babyish."

"It doesn't sound babyish," Lea said. "It sounds like you wanted your best friend, and I was busy being pleased with myself." She nudged the blue book with her toe. "This says Rogers and Farson came up with it in 1957, and they were grown men with degrees, so wanting to be understood is officially not babyish."

Chiara laughed, a short buoyant sound that popped the last of the tension. "Okay. Next time Mr. Dang picks you for something, you look at me first."

"Deal," Lea said. "And next time you go quiet, I'm going to say back what I think you mean, even if I get it wrong."

"Even if you get it really wrong," Chiara said, and leaned over to steal the blue book and flip through it herself. "Page sixty-three. Show me the part you read."

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: The 1996 book 'Continuing Bonds' argued that keeping a connection to someone who has died, through memories, objects or traditions, can be a healthy part of grieving.
story:
Victoria sat in the back row of the temple with her grandmother's blue scarf wound twice around her wrist, and she kept her eyes on the candle at the front because looking at the photo beside it made her throat close. The whole hall smelled of marigolds. James slid into the seat next to her and whispered, "You okay?" She nodded, which was not exactly true, and he seemed to know that, because he just stayed there.

After the service, everyone filed out into the courtyard, where Mrs. Okafor had set out tea and little sandwiches nobody was eating. Victoria stayed in her seat. She had been turning one question over all week, the way you turn a stone over to see what's underneath: was wearing the scarf a good thing, or was it a way of hiding from the fact that Grandma was gone? Her counselor at school had said the words "moving on" twice, and now Victoria wondered if the scarf meant she was failing at it.

Mr. Abdi, who taught science at her school and had come to the temple that morning, was stacking chairs near the front. Victoria watched him straighten one chair, then another, like a man solving a slow puzzle. She went over. "Can I ask you something weird?" she said. "If I keep wearing my grandmother's scarf, does that mean I'm not... moving on?"

Mr. Abdi rested a chair on its legs. "Moving on from what, exactly?" he asked. "Grief isn't a train you catch or miss." Then he told her about a book he'd read after his own father died, from 1996, called "Continuing Bonds." He said it had argued that keeping a connection to someone who has died, through memories, objects, or traditions, can be a healthy part of grieving. He said it in almost exactly those words, the way people repeat something that changed their mind once. Victoria held on to the sentence like a rope.

That afternoon she decided to test the idea, because that was what you did with ideas. She unwound the scarf and laid it on her bed for one hour, and she felt worse, not better, like a bear yanked out of hibernation in the middle of January. Then she put it back on and helped her father cook Grandma's rice and peas for the neighbors, following the recipe written in Grandma's cramped handwriting, and she felt something loosen in her chest instead of tighten. So the scarf was a bridge, not a cage. That was her data.

The next week she brought the rice and peas to school in a container, and James and Meadow ate it on the bleachers and said it was better than the cafeteria's gray propaganda about healthy eating, which made Victoria laugh for the first time in days. Meadow asked about the scarf, and Victoria said, "It's a continuing bond," and left it there, because some sentences you don't explain, you just wear them.

The twist came on Sunday, when she finally opened the scarf's folds all the way and something small dropped out and skittered under the pew: a folded paper, hidden in the hem where Grandma must have sewn it. Victoria knelt and pried it loose. In cramped handwriting it read, "For V, when she needs to find something I left her. Look where the poorest place in the house is richest." Victoria read it twice. Grandma had always called her little window garden "my impoverished kingdom," because it got only an hour of sun.

She ran the whole way home, scarf streaming behind her, and knelt at the window box with her fingers in the dirt. Somewhere below the marigold roots, her thumbnail hit something hard.

activity: to play a piece with dynamics and tempo changes in a band or on the piano
knowledge_domain: to play a piece with dynamics and tempo changes in a band or on the piano
fact: Tempo is measured in beats per minute, so a marking of 60 means one beat each second.
story:
Paige had been stuck on the same sixteen bars of "Moonlight Fog" for two weeks, and now she was stuck on them at Madeleine's house too, where the piano sat in a sunny room that smelled of lemon polish. The sheet music said lento at the top, then a sudden allegro halfway through, and Paige's hands refused to believe the two sections belonged to the same piece. "You're rushing the slow part," said Ivana, who had brought her practice pad and sat cross-legged on the rug with her sticks. "It's like you're scared of it."

"I'm not scared," Paige said, though her fingers were tight and she knew it. She played the opening again, and again it crept faster, the way a slippery hill creeps steeper the longer you look down it. Repeating the same sixteen bars was getting tedious, and worse, it wasn't working. Madeleine's little brother stood in the doorway radiating impatience, bouncing a tennis ball until Madeleine pointed him away with a look.

Ivana set down her sticks and squinted at the metronome marking under the word lento. "It says sixty. Do you know what that actually means?" Paige admitted she didn't, not really. Ivana tapped the wall clock above the piano. "Tempo is measured in beats per minute, so a marking of sixty means one beat each second." She pointed at the red second hand. "Watch it. Tap every time it jumps."

They all watched the clock, and Paige tapped her knee each time the hand clicked forward. One. Two. Three. It felt impossibly slow, like watching paint decide whether to dry. When she tried to play the opening at that speed, the melody changed under her hands. The chords that had sounded plain now sounded heavy and deliberate, like footsteps in fog. "That's it," Madeleine whispered from the window seat, and even the tennis ball in the hallway went quiet.

The allegro section was easier once the lento felt right, because the contrast did the work. Paige practiced the jump four times, and on the fifth try she played it straight through, slow into fast, soft into loud, without dropping a note. Ivana grabbed her sticks and played along on the practice pad, keeping the slow beat against the ticking clock until the change, when she doubled her speed and the room seemed to lift.

"Play it once more," Madeleine said, "all the way from the top, dynamics and everything." Paige flexed her fingers, glanced once at the second hand ticking its steady sixty, and began. Ivana came in beside her, and Madeleine leaned against the piano with her eyes closed, conducting the air with a pencil she'd picked up off the music stand.

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: Grief can affect the body as well as feelings, often causing tiredness, trouble sleeping or changes in appetite.
story:
At the cemetery gate Anais stopped, because for the third morning in a row the world felt foggy and her stomach turned at the thought of breakfast. She had barely slept since Grandma Rhea died, and now she was worried she was catching something on top of everything else. "You okay?" August asked, holding the folded program for the service. "I don't know," Anais said. "I haven't slept all week and I can't eat. I think I'm getting sick." The funeral started in twenty minutes, and she still had to read the poem Grandma had loved.

They walked between the headstones, cut grass sticking to her shoes, the air smelling of damp earth and lilies from the wreaths. August pointed at a flock of geese arrowing south overhead. "Your grandma was the one who knew all the birds, right?" Anais nodded. Grandma Rhea had called herself a student of migratory birds, and every October they used to sit on her porch with cocoa, counting Canada geese until their necks ached. "Migratory birds leave and come back," Anais remembered her saying, "but grandmas don't. Deal with it, girl." That had made Anais laugh, which was Grandma's whole plan.

Last night, though, there had been no laughing. She had stared at the ceiling until two, then picked at a piece of toast at seven and given up after two bites. On the walk over she had tested an idea: maybe she wasn't sick at all. Maybe this was what losing someone did to a body. She'd heard Liam mention, after his grandfather's funeral, that he couldn't eat for days and slept terribly, and then it just faded. Two examples wasn't much, but it was a pattern, and a pattern was a rule you could lean on.

"Try a few crackers," August said, digging into a jacket pocket. "Small bites. Not a whole breakfast, just fuel." Anais ate three, slowly. Her stomach accepted them. When her legs wobbled going up the little hill to the graveside, she sat for a minute on the cold bench and let the tiredness be there instead of fighting it, the way Grandma used to say you let a snowy day happen instead of battling it. "Grief is a strange adversary," Anais said. "It makes your body tired and your stomach shut down like it wants to hibernate, even though it's not even cold out."

"So you're not sick?" August asked.

"I don't think so. I think this is just what it does." She stood, the poem folded in her hand, paper soft as feathers. Mr. Tan nodded to her from the front row. Anais walked to the small podium, took a breath that smelled of lilies and rain, and began, "Because I could not stop for Death, he kindly stopped for me."

activity: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years
knowledge_domain: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years
fact: At 5 percent simple interest, $1,000 earns $50 a year, so after five years the account holds $1,250.
story:
James counted his money at the pickle stand twice, because $1,000 in twenties felt like it should weigh more than it did. He had earned it over three summers of hauling bins at the farmers' market, and now his grandmother had written him a letter, which lay folded in his back pocket like a secret.

"Read it again," said Antony, who was supposed to be stacking cucumbers for Ms. Toussaint but had drifted over. James unfolded the paper. "Dear James," he read out, "if you leave your thousand dollars with me for five years, I will pay you 5 percent simple interest. That means fifty dollars a year, so at the end you will have one thousand two hundred fifty dollars. Love, Gran." He had read it four times since breakfast, and the numbers still refused to sit still in his head.

"Fifty a year," Katarina said, arriving with a bag of peaches. "That's the same fifty every year? That's it?" James frowned at the letter. His bank had shown him a pamphlet about compound interest, where the interest earned its own interest, and Katarina had spent all of Tuesday explaining it to him while they were supposed to be pricing tomatoes. He worked it out on the back of a paper bag with Ms. Toussaint's pencil: fifty, one hundred, one hundred fifty, two hundred. "So after five years, Gran's deal gives me twelve fifty, total," he said slowly. "The bank thing would give more." Katarina shrugged. "Maybe. But your grandmother won't charge you fees, and the bank pamphlet had a picture of a sailboat on it, which I personally found suspicious. Like a counterfeit promise. All shiny, no pickle stand."

"That's a weird perspective," Antony said, "but I'm citing it forever." He stole a cucumber and pretended to study it. James looked down the row of stalls, at Ms. Toussaint arguing cheerfully with a man over the price of okra, at his grandmother's handwriting on the page. Last summer he had spent his earnings on a drone that now sat broken in his closet, and he still wasn't sure whether he regretted the buying or the crashing. Maybe giving the money to Gran for five years was just a way of locking the drone mistakes in a drawer. Or maybe it was a bad deal dressed up as a family favor.

He thought about it through the whole morning, weighing fifty a year against the bank's pamphlet and the sailboat that never sailed anywhere. At noon he texted Gran from his mother's phone: "Deal. But can we write compound into the contract for next time?" He slid the pencil back across the pickle stand to Ms. Toussaint. "You owe me one tomato," he said. "Rent for the pencil."

activity: going on a family trip away from home
knowledge_domain: going on a family trip away from home
fact: Dermatologists advise reapplying sunscreen every two hours outdoors, and immediately after swimming or sweating.
story:
Mackenzie had put on sunscreen at nine that morning, before anyone else was even awake, and by four in the afternoon her shoulders were the color of the camp stove. The family had been at the lake all day. She had swum in the morning, dried off, eaten a sandwich, swum again, played catch with Calvin from the campsite next door, and never once thought about the orange bottle sitting in the tent.

Demi crouched beside her on the picnic table bench and studied her shoulders like a detective. "You put sunscreen on this morning, right? I watched you do it."

"I did," Mackenzie said. "That's the weird part."

Demi pulled out her phone, tapped at it, and read aloud, her voice flat with disbelief. "Reapply every two hours outdoors. And immediately after swimming or sweating." She looked up. "Immediately. You swam twice."

Mackenzie tried to count backward through the day. Nine o'clock, the lotion. Ten thirty, the first swim. If the rule was every two hours, she had needed more by eleven, and the swim before that meant she'd needed it even sooner. Then lunch, then the second swim, then two hours of throwing a frisbee with Calvin in the sun. It wasn't one mistake. It was the same mistake repeated all day long, invisible until now, like a pattern you couldn't see until you stepped back from it.

"My aunt did this last summer," Demi said, peeling the label off the bottle she'd fetched from her own tent. "She said swimming washes it off, but I thought she was just being dramatic." She squirted a white ribbon into her palm. "Arms out. You're not doing this again tomorrow."

While Demi rubbed it in, Mackenzie thought about her grandmother's house, the one her parents were going to renovate next month, and how her grandmother had once told her that some things you couldn't see the damage of until later. Mackenzie had assumed she meant the pipes. Now she wondered if it was a lesson with a wider use, one she could have learned a day earlier and a lot less painfully.

Ms. Swampy, the woman who ran the camp store, walked past with a wheelbarrow of firewood and paused. "Someone spent too long in the sun?"

"Twelve hours too long," Demi said. "Roughly."

Ms. Swampy laughed and kept walking. Calvin jogged over from the water spigot holding a dripping towel and draped it, cold and heavy, across Mackenzie's shoulders without a word.

"Tomorrow," he said, "I'm setting an alarm."

activity: to write a short story with correctly punctuated dialogue and a clear climax
knowledge_domain: to write a short story with correctly punctuated dialogue and a clear climax
fact: After the climax, the falling action and resolution show the consequences of what happened and tie up the story's loose ends.
story:
Taylor had typed THE END, printed three copies, and carried them to the school library, where Jaycee and Willyam were already waiting at the corner table. The assignment from Ms. He was due Friday: a short story with correctly punctuated dialogue and a clear climax. Taylor's story was about a girl who rescued a lost dog from a storm drain, and the rescue was the big scene, all shouting and mud and the dog's wet head popping out of the pipe.

Jaycee read fast, the way she always did, and put the pages down. "The storm drain part is great. But what happened to the dog after?"

"After what?"

"After the rescue. The story just stops. Did the girl keep him? Did someone come looking for him? You said he had a collar with a tag."

Taylor had not thought about the tag since chapter one. She took the pages back and read the ending again. Two paragraphs, then THE END, and the dog was still standing in the rain. Willyam leaned over. "It's like the last piece of a puzzle is missing, and the puzzle is on the floor and nobody picks it up."

Ms. He walked past with a cart of returns and stopped when she heard the word climax. "That's the word for your loudest moment, your turning point. Your rescue scene." She shelved two books and moved on.

Taylor looked at her ending and tried a test. She wrote one new paragraph: the girl calls the number on the tag, the owner drives over in a truck with a camper shell, and the dog rides home with his head out the window. Then she wrote a second paragraph where the girl's mother says she can walk him on Saturdays. She printed the new pages and handed them to Jaycee without saying anything.

Jaycee read to the bottom. "That's better. The truck answers the tag, the Saturdays answer the girl wanting a dog. Everything gets tied up." She tapped the last line of dialogue. "Also you forgot the comma before the closing quotation mark right here."

Taylor fixed the comma. Willyam said the storm drain part still made his hands sweat, which he claimed was the highest compliment available in the library. Ms. He, passing again, glanced at the new ending and gave a small nod before pushing her cart toward biography.

Taylor saved the file twice. On Friday she got her paper back with one note in the margin: falling action and resolution do real work. She folded the paper and put it in her binder, behind the history quiz she had nearly failed, where it could insulate that particular humiliation from anyone flipping through. Then she started a new story, this time about a negligent crossing guard, and she knew exactly where the loose ends would go.

activity: going to a first school dance
knowledge_domain: going to a first school dance
fact: Ringing in the ears after loud music, called tinnitus, is a warning sign that the ears were exposed to noise loud enough to damage hearing.
story:
The gym had been transformed, more or less. Crepe paper hung from the basketball hoop like a droopy canopy, and the DJ booth sat directly under it, speakers stacked on folding chairs. Livia stood near the door with Kareem and Ireland, all three of them pretending they came to dances all the time. Then the bass dropped, and conversation became impossible.
