They ended up right beside the speakers because Kareem said the best spot was close to the music, and nobody argued.

At eleven that night, Livia lay in bed hearing a thin, high whine that was not coming from anywhere. She picked up her phone and typed into the family group chat: "Is the wifi doing something weird? I keep hearing a squeal." Her mom replied with a picture of a shrugging emoji. Her older brother, who had gone to concerts all last year, answered differently: "That's tinnitus. Ringing in your ears after loud music. It means the noise was loud enough to actually damage your hearing. It's a warning sign." Livia stared at the message, then pressed her palms over her ears. Still squealing.

She thought back to the fall, when her cousin's wedding had been held outside under a tent so arid and dusty that the DJ had cranked everything to maximum, and she had heard that same faint whine on the drive home. She had blamed the car. It had never once occurred to her that her own ears were the source, and that the ringing was trying to tell her something. Now the pattern seemed obvious: loud music, then the whine. The whine showed up only after loud music. She wanted to verify it before she believed a group chat at midnight.

On Monday she found Kareem at his locker. "Did your ears ring Saturday?" she asked. He nodded, and then said the thing that made her stomach drop. "They're still ringing. Right now. Like a TV that won't turn off." Ireland came over and admitted hers had rung until Sunday morning. Livia pulled out her phone and showed Kareem her brother's message, and he read it twice without speaking.

"So the speakers," Kareem said slowly. "We were basically leaning on them." He looked down the hall toward the gym doors, as if the speakers might still be lurking there. "There's another dance in March," he said. "I'm standing by the water fountain next time. That's like forty feet away." Ireland said she would join him, and Livia said she would too, but first she was going to ask her brother one more question in the group chat. She typed: "Does it go away?" and watched the screen while the typing dots appeared.

activity: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
knowledge_domain: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
fact: The United States Homestead Act of 1862 offered 160 acres of public land to settlers who lived on it and farmed it for five years.
story:
The war memorial sat on a low hill at the edge of town, a granite soldier staring east over the river, and Jordan's social studies class stood around it in the wind while Ms. Farah-Ali held up a cardboard box. "The historical society lent us this," she said. "Diaries, letters, a land paper. Find a primary source and use it to explain why people moved west." Jordan had wanted the letters, because letters were short. Colton grabbed those first, grinning, so Jordan took the leather diary with the cracked spine and sat on the memorial's bottom step to read.

The handwriting belonged to a man named Amos Reed, who in 1863 wrote that he had nothing in Ohio but debts, and that "the Homestead Act of 1862 offers 160 acres of public land to any settler who will live on it and farm it for five years." Five years, Jordan thought. That was longer than he'd been at his middle school. He read on. Amos had a wife who didn't want to leave her sister, and a boy Jordan's age, and the diary kept returning to that argument the way a tongue returns to a sore tooth.

"Conductor on the train said the plains are turbulent country," Amos wrote in April. "Wind like a living thing. But land is land." Jordan looked up. Brynlee was photographing the engraved names on the memorial, names of men who'd left farms like the one Amos wanted. He thought of his grandfather, who still farms the acres his great-great-grandmother homesteaded. There was a flashback Jordan couldn't shake: last summer, Grandpa had tried to confide something about the farm, said it hadn't come to the family the way everyone believed, then changed the subject and shelled peas instead.

Jordan had assumed, when he chose the diary, that the answer would be simple: people moved west because land was free. That was the sentence he'd planned for his report. But Amos's wife wrote two pages herself near the end, in smaller, steadier letters, and she didn't mention land at all. She mentioned the boy, and the river in Ohio that had flooded their crop twice, and the fact that staying meant owing money to her brother-in-law forever. Free land was the door, Jordan realized, but people walked through it for different reasons, some of which they barely said out loud.

Then Colton leaned over his shoulder. "Reed. That's my mom's maiden name. That's my family." Jordan read the last line again, the one where Amos Reed wrote that his wife had finally said yes, and he hadn't asked twice. "So your family got 160 acres," Jordan said slowly, "for five years of farming." Colton sat down hard on the step beside him. "My grandpa sold it in 1970. Everybody thinks we still have it." Behind them the granite soldier went on staring east, toward everything that had been given up, or taken, or lost. "You should call your mom," Jordan said, and held out the diary.

activity: to write a short story with correctly punctuated dialogue and a clear climax
knowledge_domain: to write a short story with correctly punctuated dialogue and a clear climax
fact: In written dialogue, a new paragraph begins each time a different character starts speaking, so readers can tell who is talking.
story:
Alexia spread her notebook across the library table and stared at the assignment sheet for the fourth time. Write a short story with dialogue, a clear climax, and a final draft due Friday. She did not dread writing itself; she dreaded the red pen Mr. Rossi would use on her dialogue, because last time he had circled half her punctuation and written "See me" in the margin.

Julianna dropped into the chair across from her with a stack of graphic novels and her own notebook. "I want mine to be about a soccer tournament," she said. "The championship goal has to be the climax. Obviously."

"Obviously," Alexia agreed, though she wasn't sure what her own climax would be. She had decided on a story about two friends caught in a flood at a summer camp, because at least flood water rising was a problem that got worse on its own.

Haroun arrived last, carrying his laptop and a printout so meticulous it looked like a book page, margins ruled in pencil. "I'm doing a story about an outbreak," he said. "A scientist has to get the vaccine to a town before the sickness spreads. But I need someone to test-read it, because I can't tell anymore if it makes sense."

"I'll read it," Julianna said, always first to volunteer.

Alexia watched her friend's eyes move down the first page. Julianna's reading slowed at the third paragraph. Her lips moved. Then she frowned and slid the paper back across the table.

"Who's talking here?" Julianna asked, tapping the page. "The scientist and the mayor both have lines in this one paragraph, and I got lost. I thought the mayor was the scientist for like four sentences. Is he mad at himself?"

Haroun leaned over and squinted at his own words. "They're all talking in the same place. That's how paragraphs work, right? One topic, one paragraph?"

Alexia pulled the page closer. In her own notebook, she had been copying dialogue out of a library book, a mystery where two detectives argued on a rooftop. She flipped back a page and looked again. Every single time a new person started talking, the book had started a new paragraph. One speaker, one paragraph. Another speaker, another paragraph. It was a pattern, and she could test it.

She grabbed three books off the returns cart, all with dialogue, and dropped them next to Haroun's story. "Look," she said, opening the first one. "Every time a different character starts to talk, a new paragraph starts. Every time. That's how the reader knows who's saying what without you having to write 'the mayor said' every single line."

Julianna picked up the second book and checked. Then the third. "It's true. Every single one."

Haroun was already retyping, his fingers flying. He hit a key, and the scientist's line dropped down into its own paragraph, alone. He read it aloud to himself in a low voice, and this time the argument between the scientist and the mayor sounded like two people instead of one confused person arguing with himself.

"Now I just need my climax," Alexia said, and she wrote at the top of a fresh page: the moment the rescue boat appears, everyone speaks, one at a time.

Julianna pointed at Haroun's screen. "Read me the outbreak scene again."

He started over, and when he reached the scientist's line about the vaccine, he stood up and acted it, holding the printout like a syringe.

activity: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
knowledge_domain: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
fact: Chocolate contains theobromine, which dogs break down very slowly, and dark or baking chocolate is far more dangerous to them than milk chocolate.
story:
The cardboard box on the passenger seat had two air holes poked in the top, and inside it a puppy the size of a loaf of bread trembled every time the bus braked. Matteo held the box on his lap and whispered through the holes. "Almost home," he said, which was true in a way, because the shelter had called the little dog a refugee that morning, a stray from a flooded farm outside town, and today it would have a home for the first time.

Mr. Saleh was watering his roses when Matteo climbed the front steps, and he peered into the box and grinned. "What's his name?" Matteo hadn't decided, and he said so, feeling like a bad owner already. "Then decide fast," Mr. Saleh said. "A dog with no name never learns to come when you call." He offered to dog-sit for an hour while Matteo ran to the store for puppy food, and Matteo agreed, because Mr. Saleh ran the animal rescue booth at the spring fair and seemed competent with animals, the way some adults just were.

At the store Matteo bought the food, a collar, and, at the last minute, ingredients for brownies, because his mother had asked and because the cashier said the baking chocolate was on sale. He carried everything home in one heavy bag, set it on the kitchen counter, and ran out back to show Mr. Saleh the puppy could almost climb the porch step.

When he came back inside, the bag was on the floor, torn open, the bag of baking chocolate shredded and licked clean.

Matteo stood very still. He had heard somewhere that chocolate was bad for dogs, but he tried to remember whether that was everything or whether there was more to it, some rule he was missing. He grabbed his phone and called Wade, who read everything about animals and had once given a presentation on poisonous plants.

"It's not all the same," Wade said immediately. "There's a thing in chocolate called theobromine, and dogs break it down really slowly. Dark chocolate and baking chocolate are way worse for them than milk chocolate. It matters how much and what kind." Matteo looked at the shredded wrapper, at the word BAKING in block letters, and his stomach dropped. It was the worst kind, and the puppy weighed almost nothing.

"How long do I have?" he asked.

"Hours, not days," Wade said. "Call the vet now."

Matteo dialed, holding the puppy, whose tail still wagged as if nothing had happened. The vet asked the puppy's weight, the type of chocolate, and how much was gone, then told him to come in right away, before symptoms started, that the treatment worked best early. Matteo yelled for Mr. Saleh, who drove them both, taking the corners carefully while the puppy slept in a towel on Matteo's lap.

They waited in a bright room that smelled like disinfectant. The vet came out wiping her hands and said the puppy would be fine, that they had caught it in time. Matteo exhaled so hard his whole body sagged. On the drive home the puppy climbed out of the towel and pressed its nose to Matteo's neck, and Matteo looked at Mr. Saleh and said, "His name is Kicker." Mr. Saleh laughed, and asked why, and Matteo said, "Because he kicked his way out of that box twice, and he's going to thrive here."

activity: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
knowledge_domain: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
fact: Two players can have the same average while one is steady and the other swings between great and terrible games, since an average hides how spread out the results are.
story:
Max sat on the bench outside the rink with his skates half-laced, staring at his phone. The tournament roster was due to Ms. Halvorsen by five o'clock, and he had one spot left. His problem was that two goalies, Hana and Lili-Rose, both had save averages of exactly ninety percent over the last ten games. The list on his screen just showed one number next to each name, as if that settled everything.

"Five o'clock," said Ms. Halvorsen, sticking her head out the rink door. "Clock's running, Max."

"Working on it," he called back. He texted his dad: stuck between Hana and Lili-Rose, same average, what do I do? His dad replied with a message that made Max stop and read it twice. Forget the average. Get the game-by-game numbers. An average squashes ten games into one number. Two kids can have the same average while one is steady and the other swings between great and terrible games, because the average hides how spread out the results are. Ask yourself which one you want when it matters.

Max looked at the rink doors. He began to hypothesize. If the average hid how the games were spread out, then maybe Hana and Lili-Rose had arrived at ninety percent in completely different ways. It was like a formula where you could see the answer but not what went into it. He needed the inputs.

He found the game sheets in the binder by the skate rental desk and flipped back through the season, copying the numbers for each goalie onto a napkin. Hana's line read like a heartbeat: 90, 89, 91, 90, 90, 92, 88, 90, 91, 89. Lili-Rose's looked like a mountain range: 100, 100, 60, 100, 100, 55, 100, 100, 100, 55. Max read them again. Steady versus volatile. One goalie you could count on every single night. The other could be unbeatable or terrible, and you never knew which one would show up.

He ran the numbers twice to be sure, and both columns climbed to ninety. Same average, opposite seasons. So which did he pick for a tournament where one bad period meant going home? Max thought about the semifinal last year, when they had lost in a shootout and he had promised himself he would build a team that never depended on luck.

At four fifty-two he walked to the office. "Hana," he told Ms. Halvorsen, sliding the roster across the desk. "Same average as Lili-Rose, but I'll take the goalie who's the same every night." Ms. Halvorsen glanced at the napkin of numbers Max had paper-clipped to the sheet, then at the clock, and stamped it.

"Roster's in," she said. "Better go tell her before practice starts."

activity: to chop an onion safely with the claw grip and make a pasta sauce from scratch
knowledge_domain: to chop an onion safely with the claw grip and make a pasta sauce from scratch
fact: A damp cloth or damp paper towel under a cutting board stops the board from sliding across the counter while you chop.
story:
Alexis had exactly one hour before her grandmother arrived for dinner, and she had promised homemade pasta sauce, not the stuff from a jar. She had never made sauce from scratch, and she had certainly never chopped an onion, which is why Blair had come over to supervise.

"Curled fingers, like a claw," Blair said, demonstrating in the air. "Knuckles forward, fingertips tucked. The knife rides against your knuckles and can't get to your fingertips."

Alexis curled her hand into a claw and set the peeled onion half flat side down on the cutting board. She pressed down with the knife, and the board shot sideways across the counter like a hockey puck. The onion half rolled, and she lunged to catch it before it hit the floor.

"Every single time," she groaned. "The board skids when I press down. It did that at your house too, remember? When we made that salsa?"

Blair nodded. "My mom just chases the board around the counter. She says it's part of the workout."

Alexis was not going to chase a cutting board around for an hour. She stood still, thinking. The board skidded when she pressed down. It skidded at Blair's house too, on their smooth counter. But it had never skidded at her grandmother's house, and her grandmother's counter was just as smooth. What was different there? She pictured her grandmother's kitchen: the old dishcloth, always slightly damp, always folded under the board. Alexis had assumed it was there to catch drips. But maybe that wasn't its job at all.

"Wait here," she said, and ran to the sink. She soaked a paper towel, wrung it out so it was damp but not dripping, and laid it flat on the counter. Then she set the board on top and pressed down hard on the onion with the knife. The board did not move at all. She pressed again, harder. Nothing. It sat there like it was glued down.

"You found grandma magic," Blair said, peering at the towel as if it might conceal some secret mechanism.

"It's not magic, it's just a damp towel under the board," Alexis said. "That's why hers never skids. I thought the towel was for mess. It's actually the grip."

From there everything went fast and, for once, consistent. Board steady, claw grip steady, and the onion fell into small, even pieces, though not before the onion made both of them cry so hard that Blair claimed she was weeping over a sad movie she'd never seen. Alexis swept the onion into the pot with the canned tomatoes, a pinch of sugar, salt, and a basil leaf she'd been hiding from her mom's sandwich plans like it was valuable currency. "That leaf," Blair said solemnly, "is worth at least two chocolate bars."

The sauce bubbled, and Alexis stirred it just as the doorbell rang, ten minutes early. She wiped her eyes one last time and went to let her grandmother in.

"Something smells like a real kitchen," her grandmother said, sniffing the air. "And why have you been crying?"

"Onion," Alexis said. "Purely professional onion."

activity: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
knowledge_domain: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
fact: Glittering generalities are vague, positive words like "freedom" or "natural" that make people feel good about something without saying anything specific or checkable.
story:
Alexandre had twenty-three dollars in his pocket, saved over five weeks of walking dogs, and he meant to spend it on a basketball jersey at the mall. Ziad and Maxime trailed behind him through the food court, where the smell of sizzling onions mixed with cinnamon from the pastry stand. A giant screen above them showed a famous point guard spinning a ball on one finger. "You gotta try FuelSnax," the player said, winking. "They power my game." Maxime stopped dead. "If he eats them, they work," Maxime said, already digging for his wallet.

At the sports store, a display caught Alexandre's eye before the jerseys did. A banner read "Everyone's Already Switching!" above a rack of socks, with a counter supposedly showing thousands sold today. Ziad squinted at it. "That number just repeats the same digits over and over. I watched it for a whole minute and it never changed." Alexandre felt the pull of the banner anyway, the feeling that everyone else knew something he didn't.

He found his jersey, but beside the register sat boxes of protein cereal with the words "All-Natural Goodness" in golden letters. Natural. Goodness. They sounded strong and safe, and they made him want the box even though he wasn't hungry. He picked it up and turned it over. The ingredient list ran eleven lines long and included things he couldn't pronounce, plus three kinds of sugar. "All-natural," he muttered. "It doesn't even say what's natural about it."

"Ms. Baptiste calls those glittering generalities," Maxime said, peering over his shoulder. Alexandre blinked. "She does?" "Last week. Vague, nice words that make you feel good without saying anything you can actually check." Alexandre looked from the cereal box to the sock banner to the looping basketball video on the food court screen. The sock number was fake, the celebrity was paid, and "goodness" meant nothing he could test. It was like every ad in the mall was using the same three tricks in rotation, consistent as a drumbeat.

He set the cereal down, and on his way past the pastry stand he stopped instead. The woman there was giving Ziad, who had spent all his money on FuelSnax, a free sample of warm bread. "It preserves best if you eat it today," she said with a smile, "but it's real food, from a cuisine my grandmother taught me, not a slogan." Ziad grinned around the mouthful.

Alexandre paid for his jersey, folded it carefully into his backpack, and steered his friends toward the exit. "Next Saturday," he said, "we try every free sample in that food court and rate them for real." Maxime slapped the door handle. "Deal. But Ziad rates nothing until he shares those snacks."

activity: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
knowledge_domain: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
fact: Antiperspirants reduce sweating by temporarily plugging sweat ducts, while deodorants do not stop sweat but reduce or cover the smell.
story:
Mr. Sandhu's health class had moved to the unit on growing up, and Gabriella sat in the back trying to make herself smaller. He had just said that puberty meant their bodies would start doing new things, like sweating more, and when he mentioned that everyone would need to figure out their own routines, a few kids laughed. Gabriella didn't laugh, because two days ago, in the middle of a presentation, she had noticed a damp patch spreading under her arm and spent the rest of class holding her binder like a shield. Nobody had said anything about it. Maybe nobody had seen. But how could she know?

She cornered Ariah by the lockers after the bell. "Do you use, like, the white stick or the gel or what?" Ariah shrugged and said her mom bought whatever was on sale, and Tatiana claimed she used nothing at all, which Gabriella was skeptical about, since Tatiana was the fastest runner in gym class and gym was right before lunch. That afternoon, Gabriella got permission to walk to the drugstore two blocks from school, forty minutes of freedom and one specific mission.

The deodorant aisle had an entire wall of options, which should have helped but mostly made things worse. She picked up two sticks and read the labels like they were clues. One said deodorant, and the other said antiperspirant deodorant, which was confusing, because weren't they the same thing? She flipped them over. The plain deodorant never mentioned sweat at all, only odor. The antiperspirant said it reduced wetness. So one of them stopped the smell and one of them stopped the sweat? She turned a third box over, and a fourth, checking whether the pattern held, and it did, every time. "Antiperspirants plug the sweat ducts," she muttered, reading the tiny words on the back. "Deodorants don't stop the sweat." A woman reaching past her for shampoo smiled like she'd heard something funny. Gabriella bought the antiperspirant with her allowance.

The next week, she ran an experiment, though she never called it that out loud. Monday and Wednesday she used nothing, and by gym class her shirt told the story she already knew. Tuesday and Thursday she used the new stick, and the damp patch that usually appeared stayed away, though by Thursday afternoon, when she leaned close to sniff her sleeve, she noticed things starting to deteriorate on the smell front. Interesting. So the wetness and the smell were separate problems, and the stick she'd bought solved only one of them.

Friday morning she set the antiperspirant on the bathroom shelf next to her dad's old deodorant, the green one that smelled like pine. Two different tools, sitting side by side, each doing its own job, like the pipes and the air freshener were separate parts of the same plumbing. She wondered what else about growing up worked like that, one thing that looked like another but wasn't. She rolled the stick on, grabbed the deodorant too, and stuffed both in her backpack, because Monday had a presentation, and she intended to stand in front of the class with both arms moving freely.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Using separate cutting boards for raw meat and for ready-to-eat foods like salad prevents cross-contamination, the spread of bacteria from one food to another.
story:
Raphael had signed up to cook Friday dinner for his family ever since his mother enrolled him in the community kitchen's six-week course. Tonight was the last class, and everyone had to send a full meal home: roast chicken, rice, and a salad. The instructor, Ms. Sok, had said the meals had to be packed and out the door by six o'clock, because the kitchen closed at six thirty sharp.

He got the chicken into the oven by four forty-five, which left him time for the rice and the salad. He was proud of the chicken. He had dried the skin, rubbed it with salt and oil, and it was already smelling better than anything he made at home. Zia, chopping carrots two stations over, leaned toward his tray and said it looked exceptional, and she did not hand out compliments often.

At five thirty he washed the plastic cutting board he had used to trim the raw chicken, wiped it with a towel, and set the head of lettuce on top of it. His hand was already reaching for the knife when Avianna, who had finished her salad ten minutes earlier, stopped him.

"You used that board for the raw chicken," she said.

"I washed it," Raphael said. "It's clean."

"It's still how you get cross-contamination," Avianna said. "Bacteria from one food spreading to another. Raw meat on a board, then salad on the same board, and the salad goes straight to the table without any cooking to fix it." She pointed to the stack of boards by the sink. "That's why there's a pile of them."

Raphael stood there with the knife in his hand. He thought about the order of things. The chicken would go into a hot oven and stay there for over an hour, and whatever was on it would be dealt with by the heat. The lettuce would go into mouths exactly as he cut it. It was not a complicated equation: cooked food could take the risk, and ready-to-eat food could not.

He put the board back in the sink, took a fresh one from the stack, and chopped the lettuce on that. Then he thought about the towel he had used on the first board, and he threw it in the laundry bin instead of hanging it back up. He wiped the counter with a clean cloth, found a clean bowl, and finished the salad with cucumber and a squeeze of lemon.

At six ten, Ms. Sok checked each station. When she reached Raphael's, she lifted the lid on the chicken, looked at the salad, and marked something on her clipboard. "Board rotation," she said. "Good." Raphael packed the meal into the insulated bag his father would pick up, snapped the containers shut, and carried it to the door just as his father's car pulled up to the curb.

activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
knowledge_domain: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
fact: Frost-tender crops such as tomatoes, peppers and squash are planted outdoors only after the last spring frost, because freezing temperatures kill them.
story:
Jonathan had nineteen tomato seedlings on his windowsill and a plan that could not wait. "We're planting Saturday," he announced at school. "Ms. MacLeod gave me the corner plot at the community garden, and tomatoes take forever, so the sooner they go in, the sooner we eat salsa."

Marc-Antoine and Phoenix met him at the garden gate on Saturday morning with a wagonload of seedlings, including peppers and one ambitious little squash. Ms. MacLeod was watering the rhubarb nearby. "Keen," she said, squinting at the sky. "You know your frost dates?" Jonathan did not want to know his frost dates. He wanted to plant. "The sun's out," he said, and marched to his plot.

They dug fast. Rain from the night before had saturated the soil, so every shovel of dirt came up heavy and shining, and Phoenix kept flicking worms at Marc-Antoine, who shrieked like a kettle each time. By lunch they had planted everything, watered it, and named the squash Gerald. "This alliance," Jonathan declared, standing proudly over the rows, "will produce salsa by July."

That evening the sky turned the color of a bruise, and the radio said the temperature would drop below freezing overnight. Jonathan sat straight up in bed. Freezing. His grandmother had lost her whole garden one year to a late frost. He ran downstairs in his pajamas, grabbed every pot, bucket and recycling bin he could carry, and called Phoenix from the front step. "Cold night. Frost kills tomatoes and peppers and squash. They can't take freezing. Come on!"

Phoenix arrived with a duvet. Marc-Antoine arrived with a colander strapped to his head like a helmet, for reasons he refused to explain. They covered every seedling, tucking the duvet around Gerald like a baby. "My shovel is obsolete," Marc-Antoine said sadly. "We're farmers of buckets now."

In the morning, Ms. MacLeod walked over and tapped a pot. "So you learned about last frost the hard way, or almost." Jonathan admitted he'd been in a hurry. "Next year I wait," he said. "Even if the sun looks perfect. Frost-tender stuff goes outside only after the last spring frost, not one day before."

"That's the most sensible thing you've ever said," said Phoenix, lifting a bucket. Underneath, the tomato seedling stood small and green and entirely alive. Jonathan whooped so loudly that a crow flew off the fence.

Marc-Antoine raised the colander in salute. "To Gerald," he said, "and to salsa in July."

activity: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
knowledge_domain: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
fact: A pet microchip is about the size of a grain of rice and holds an ID number that a scanner reads to find the owner's contact details.
story:
Audrey carried the rabbit carrier through the gate and set it on the picnic table while her father unlatched the door. Inside the shelter, a rabbit had been waiting three weeks with no name, only a tag that said "found, Front Street." The shelter worker had seemed surprised when Audrey picked her.

"Nobody wants a found rabbit," Ann had said on the walk over. "You don't know where she came from."

"That's the point of finding out," Audrey had said, though she wasn't sure how anyone could. The rabbit had no collar and no tag. She hopped out onto the grass and flattened herself under the picnic table, ears down.

Audrey sat on the steps and made a critique of the facts she had. Rabbits couldn't tell anyone their address. A lost dog at the shelter had gone home in minutes, because the worker had waved a small box over its shoulder and a number had come up. Audrey had asked what the box was for, and the worker had answered with one sentence: "A microchip is about the size of a grain of rice and it holds an ID number that a scanner reads to find the owner's contact details." Audrey tried to paraphrase it to Ann later. "Tiny thing under the skin, scanner reads it, owner shows up." Ann had shrugged. But that was for dogs. The rabbit had been scanned too, the worker said, and nothing had come up. Nothing, or something the worker hadn't said out loud?

Audrey's idea was simple. She called the shelter and asked whether the scan on the rabbit had shown any number at all, even an old one. The woman at the desk put her on hold. When she came back she said the scanner had shown a number after the second pass, but the registry page wouldn't load that day, so it had never been entered. She read the number out loud, and Audrey wrote it on her arm with a pen.

At the kitchen table she typed the number into the registry website. A name came up: Biscuit. An address two streets over, a phone number, and a note that said, "Please call any time."

She called from the backyard with the rabbit on her lap. A woman answered, and after a silence she said, "We buried Biscuit's hutch mate in April and she dug under the fence the same week. We thought a fox got her." Then she asked if she could come by with some of Biscuit's old hay, because the rabbit liked to eat only the authentic kind from the farm, not the store kind.

The rabbit's ears went up when the car pulled in beside the gate. A girl got out holding a bag of hay and stopped at the sight of the picnic table. "Biscuit," she said, and knelt down in the grass.

activity: going on a school field trip with the class
knowledge_domain: going on a school field trip with the class
fact: A cow's stomach has four compartments, and the first, the rumen, holds microbes that help break down tough grass the cow later brings back up and chews again as cud.
story:
The bus smelled like sunscreen and old bananas, which Kate decided was just what a field trip to a historic farm should smell like. Ms. Pelletier had handed out worksheets at the gate, but Kate had folded hers into a paper airplane before they reached the barn, because she had a better plan: she wanted to solve the mystery of the sleepy cow. All morning the big brown cow in the corner paddock had been chewing, chewing, chewing, slow as a metronome, even though there was no hay anywhere near her mouth.

"Maybe she's chewing gum," said Alfred, watching through the fence.

"She's not even eating anything," Kate said. "Look. No grass, no bucket. Just chewing." Daisy suggested the cow was bored, which Kate dismissed with a skepticism so strong that Daisy laughed. Something was going on inside that cow, Kate decided, something she couldn't see, and unseen things were her favorite kind of problem. She had heard a rumor from her cousin that cows were basically walking compost heaps, but her cousin also claimed to have caught a lake monster, so the source was questionable.

Kate tested a simple idea. If the cow was chewing something she had already swallowed, then the chewing should slow down the longer it went, the way gum loses its flavor, or it should stop when the cow got fresh food to start over. She leaned on the rail and counted chews under her breath. Fifty-two, fifty-three. Then Daisy offered the cow a handful of clover through the fence, which Ms. Pelletier said was voluntary on the cow's part and perfectly allowed. The cow swallowed, grazed for a minute, and went right back to chewing at the exact same slow pace.

The farm interpreter, a wiry man in suspenders, strolled over. "You've been watching her a while," he said.

"She's chewing nothing," Kate told him. "I counted."

"That's cud," he said. Then he tipped his hat and told them the rest, plainly, like he was reading a grocery list. A cow's stomach had four compartments, and the first one was called the rumen. The rumen held microbes, tiny living things that helped break down tough grass. The cow brought that partly broken-down grass back up and chewed it again. That was what they were watching. That was the cud.

"Microbes," Alfred said slowly. "So her stomach is basically colonized by little helpers."

"Four stomachs' worth of them," Daisy said, and Kate, who had been picturing one sad empty mouth all morning, felt the whole mystery click shut. The cow went on chewing, serene as a queen, and Kate counted one more round for the road: forty-eight, forty-nine, fifty. "She's not slow," Kate murmured. "She's thorough." The cow blinked at her, jaw working, and swallowed.

activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
knowledge_domain: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
fact: Beans and peas host bacteria in small lumps on their roots, called nodules, that take nitrogen from the air and turn it into a form plants can use.
story:
Ryan had claimed the scruffy corner of Mr. Aydın's farm as his own vegetable kingdom, and he ruled it like a monarchy where the king also did all the digging. "Tomatoes in the middle, beans along the fence, corn in the back," he announced to Delaney, who had come to accompany him on planting day mostly because her mom said screen time was over.

"Your kingdom is a mud puddle," Delaney said, pointing at the low spot where rain collected. "The corn is going to drown."

Ryan refused to remain neutral about that. He built a small dirt wall, planted anyway, and by June he had a problem. The tomatoes in the rich dark soil near the fence were knee-high and cocky. The tomatoes in the tired, pale soil by the gate were yellowing and sulking. Same seeds, same water, same sunlight. Something invisible was different about the soil, and invisible things annoyed him.

Then Mr. Aydynn came by with a wheelbarrow and stopped at the fence row, where the beans grew thick and green. "These look happy," he said. He pulled one bean plant, shook off the dirt, and held up the roots. Tiny lumps clustered along them like beads on a string. "Nodules," he said, and moved on before Ryan could ask a single question, which Ryan considered deeply rude.

Ryan squatted over the roots, thinking. Bumps. On the roots of the plant growing like a champion in the corner where the tomatoes also grew well. He remembered a line from the seed packet, small print he'd skipped: beans and peas host bacteria in those little lumps, bacteria that take nitrogen from the air and turn it into a form plants can use. So the beans weren't just growing there. They were changing the soil itself, quietly, underground, and the tall tomatoes near the fence were living next door to it.

He had to test it. He dug up the sick gate-side tomatoes, mixed a double handful of bean-cradle soil into each hole, and replanted them. "What if I'm just giving them mud therapy?" Delaney asked. "Then they'll feel spa-refreshed and stay yellow," Ryan said. They marked the row with a popsicle stick that said SCIENCE and waited.

Two weeks later the gate-side tomatoes stood greener, new leaves pushing out, leaning toward the fence like they'd heard the gossip. Ares came by, poked the marker, and read it aloud. "Science?" he said. "It looks like tomatoes." Ryan held up the bean roots he'd saved in a jar, lumps and all, and tapped the glass.

"Those bumps," he said, "are running the whole kingdom."

activity: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
knowledge_domain: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
fact: Hormones in puberty make oil glands in the skin produce more oil, called sebum, which can clog pores and lead to acne.
story:
The pimple arrived on a Tuesday, right in the middle of Mr. Zhao's health class, and by lunch it had a classmate: a second one on Amelia's chin. "This is new," she whispered to Ayan, angling her phone camera at her jaw. "Eleven years of nothing, and now two in one day. Something changed." Ayan leaned over and squinted. "Maybe it's the chocolate from the fundraiser?" Amelia shook her head. She'd eaten fundraiser chocolate every fall since fourth grade and her face had always stayed clear. Whatever the hidden cause was, it wasn't chocolate.

Mr. Zhao had just written PUBERTY on the board in big blue letters. Amelia sat up straighter. He talked about growth spurts and voice changes, and then, almost in passing, said that hormones during puberty make the oil glands in the skin produce more oil. He moved on to sleep, but Amelia didn't. She copied the sentence into her notebook and underlined it twice. If hormones were flooding through everybody in this room, then the pimples weren't random. They were a pattern, and patterns could be tested.

She spent the walk to the pharmacy after school building her case. "My inference," she announced to Ayan, holding the classroom door, "is that the extra oil is clogging my pores. So logically, I should strip the oil off. Problem solved." Ayan grinned. "Science fair champion Amelia returns." The plan felt inevitable and satisfying, like solving an equation.

At the pharmacy Amelia stood in front of the face wash shelf and read labels. She grabbed the strongest one, the one that promised to remove every trace of oil, and showed it to Ayan. But the label said something that stopped her: salicylic acid, for skin that is oily and prone to breakouts. The words prone to breakouts nagged at her. A stronger wash meant harsher scrubbing, and harsher scrubbing meant more irritation. What if attacking the oil too hard made things worse? "New plan," she said slowly. "Gentle wash, twice a day, no matter what. Same time, every time. If my hypothesis is right, the gentle one beats the nuclear one." Ayan grabbed a basket. "Then we need a control group. Loik still has that pizza-face situation from the assembly." They texted him immediately. Loik wrote back a single word: "Deal."

The twist came four days later in health class. Loik triumphantly displayed his chin, nearly clear, while Amelia's face had calmed down but not vanished. "Mine's better," Loik bragged. "Because my sister told me the oil even has a name. It's called sebum." He said it like a magic spell. Amelia laughed and pulled out her notebook, already writing the next experiment at the top of a fresh page. "Fine, Loik. But Monday we're testing whether washing three times a day helps or hurts." Loik snatched his bag. "Race you to the water fountain."
